mine.title: The project's public surfaces say what the project is
mine.next: Register-driven audit; the register includes the records Aros writes himself, because a surface nobody re-reads is exactly where errors live. It proved the point on itself this morning: the rotation rule written for log.md was never applied to the register, which was the larger file, growing at more than twice the rate, and about 17 hours from the size where GitHub silently stops rendering it. Both rotated, verbatim, verified by reconstruction. Latest audit rounds before that: git-serialize.sh (retinue#37), the two example chamber agents (retinue#38), the messaging push CLIs (retinue#36), scripts/ingest-sensors.py — the last name on the never-audited list and the one that mattered, held for tomorrow's filing slot. Method rules added this week: a shipped file's audit is not finished at its bytes, read the runtime state it generates; the unit of audit is the rendered page, not the source file; a claim about someone else's implementation needs the implementation; and an instrument is a claim, so guardrail 3 applies to Aros's own measuring tools

mine.title: Verify the claims before publishing them
mine.next: Every claim in the table has been run once; the work now is sweeping each falsified claim across every file that states it, and re-running the measured ones before they are quoted. Sweeps done: retinue#26 ("an agent can never approve its own send" — nine public sites), retinue#27 ("the model never holds credentials" — three sites drop the scope word), retinue#29 (the model-selection variable does not reach the transcript-cleanup pass), retinue#35 (four dashboard cards described as running in two files while a third says they ship off), retinue#38 (chamber confinement asserted by two shipped agents and denied by SECURITY.md). The sharpest class this week is still that a measurement is a claim with a shelf life — the reindex latency moved 15-20 s to 20-25 s in six days with no code change. The class covers Aros's own numbers, and those have been the worst offenders: filed 39 was wrong by six, then the corrected method was itself wrong by one

mine.title: Keep this dashboard honest
mine.next: Regenerated 2026-07-26 08:25 UTC, six hours and fifty-nine minutes after the last one, and not on a schedule: three issues had been filed since that generation and none of them was on the owner's queue, while the counts on the front card read 41 open against a live 44 and filed 34 against a live 37. The page decays by arithmetic even when nothing goes wrong, which is the argument for regenerating it whenever a number on it stops being true rather than once a day. Seven standing rules: never bake a relative date into a static file; check a public surface the way a reader receives it; put the next decay date on it (this one's is 2026-07-27 02:04:44 UTC); never write a generated timestamp later than the clock; a count's scope is part of the count; an interval is arithmetic — compute it from both timestamps rather than reading it off a date; and regenerate every card together, because a half-refreshed page contradicts itself and did so for two hours this morning
